title: Silence and Radiators
premise: Quentin Coldharbour has spent twenty years writing postcards to 14 Marrow Lane, the house that burned down with his childhood inside it, signing them with names that aren't his. When the scorched lot is auctioned by his estranged aunt, he returns to the family he fled, only to find they've all arranged their lives around a single unspoken question: what really happened the night of the fire. As Quentin's postcards surface one by one in an estate box, each relative believes a different sibling wrote them, and the family's fragile loyalties begin to fracture. In the end Quentin confesses that he set the fire himself as a child to destroy evidence of his father's crimes, and the family must choose between the comfortable silence and the painful truth; they choose truth, and rebuild—not the house, but each other.
about_author: G. M. Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered mail in a northern English postal museum. Their debut novel was shortlisted for the Halloway Prize for first fiction.

chapters.title: The Address That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Quentin, who mails his 214th postcard to a burned-down address and perfects the smile that ends conversations at the post office. A solicitor's letter arrives: 14 Marrow Lane is being auctioned. Beat: routine cracked open.

chapters.title: Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. He studies the auction listing and recognizes his aunt Vera's handwriting in the lot description. He tells no one, but buys a train ticket home for the first time in twenty years. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: The Family That Arranged Itself
chapters.summary: Vera's POV. She prepares the house sale and reflects on how the family stopped asking questions after the fire, each member assigned a silence. She recognizes Quentin on the platform but says nothing. Beat: complicity revealed.

chapters.title: Postcard, Unsigned
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. At the viewing, he finds an estate box containing dozens of his own postcards—returned, hoarded, read. Someone in the family has known about them for years. Beat: exposure begins.

chapters.title: Brother of Ash
chapters.summary: Older brother Daniel's POV. Daniel confronts Quentin privately, certain the postcards are Vera's doing, and warns him not to 'reopen the cold cases.' Beat: loyalty asserted over truth.

chapters.title: Sister of Smoke
chapters.summary: Sister Imogen's POV. Imogen, who left for Australia the year after the fire, returns for the auction and greets Quentin like no time has passed—a warmth that terrifies him because she remembers everything. Beat: tenderness as threat.

chapters.title: What the Neighbours Kept
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. An elderly neighbour, Mrs. Pell, shows him photographs from the night of the fire, including one of a child's silhouette at an upstairs window. Quentin realizes someone saw him that night. Beat: the past closes in.

chapters.title: The Question Under the Table
chapters.summary: Family dinner scene, rotating close-third among siblings. Everyone circles the unspoken question; Daniel proposes a toast to 'the house' and the table goes silent. Beat: tension ratchets without a word spoken.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Burned Room
chapters.summary: Imogen's POV. She searches the ruins before the auction and finds the foundation of the old cellar door her father always kept locked. She pockets a melted key. Beat: discovery with consequences.

chapters.title: Two Truths, One Fire
chapters.summary: Daniel and Imogen argue in alternating POV fragments. Daniel insists the fire was an accident of wiring; Imogen produces the key and asks why their father locked a cellar full of ledgers. Beat: the official story cracks.

chapters.title: The Postman's Testimony
chapters.summary: Mrs. Pell's POV. She recalls delivering postcards addressed to a dead house for two decades and finally connects the handwriting to young Quentin. She says nothing yet, but writes him a letter. Beat: an outside witness enters the conspiracy of silence.

chapters.title: Midnight at Marrow Lane
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. He breaks into the lot at night to retrieve the postcards before the auction, but Imogen is already there with the key. They open the cellar together and find the ledgers documenting their father's fraud. Beat: alliance formed in secret.

chapters.title: What Father Buried
chapters.summary: Imogen's POV. The ledgers reveal their father laundered money through neighbours' savings, and the fire destroyed the proof. The siblings realize the whole town lost something that night. Beat: stakes widen beyond family.

chapters.title: Daniel's Bargain
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Daniel offers to buy the lot quietly and burn the ledgers, protecting the family name—and revealing he's suspected the truth for years and chose silence. Beat: antagonist turn rooted in love.

chapters.title: The Letter from Mrs. Pell
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Mrs. Pell's letter arrives: she saw a boy leave the burning house carrying a tin box, and she never told. Quentin understands she protected him then and is offering him the choice now. Beat: mercy as pressure.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Ensemble scene, mostly Vera's POV. Bidding opens; Daniel intends to win and bury everything. Quentin stands up in front of the whole assembled family and neighbourhood and bids against his brother—with words, not money. Beat: public rupture.

chapters.title: The Smile Fails
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Cornered before the crowd, Quentin tries the smile that ends conversations and it doesn't work. He begins to say what happened the night of the fire. Beat: climax threshold.

chapters.title: Confession at Fourteen Marrow Lane
chapters.summary: Quentin's full confession, intercut with the family's reactions: he set the fire at eleven years old to destroy his father's ledgers and protect his mother, who had discovered the fraud. Beat: climax—the question answered.

chapters.title: The Verdict of the Table
chapters.summary: Rotating POV across all four siblings and Vera. Each must respond to the truth: Daniel storms out, Imogen weeps with relief, Vera admits she always knew and stayed silent longest. Beat: fallout, raw and unresolved.

chapters.title: What We Do With Ashes
chapters.summary: Imogen's POV. Weeks later, the family votes on the lot: not to rebuild, but to make it a small garden and reading room with the ledgers displayed honestly. Daniel returns, not forgiven but present. Beat: turning toward repair.

chapters.title: Last Postcard, First Address
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. He writes one final postcard—to his new address, signed with his own name for the first time—and mails it to himself. Beat: identity reclaimed.

chapters.title: Silence, Radiating Warmth
chapters.summary: Ensemble epilogue at the garden's opening. The family sits together in the quiet, which is now chosen rather than imposed; Mrs. Pell cuts the ribbon. Beat: resolution—found family rebuilt on truth.
